problems.title: Maximum live
problems.statement: Straight-line code (each line defines one value): a = …; b = …; c = a + b; d = a · 2; e = c + d; f = b + 1; g = e + f. g is the result.

parts.prompt: Maximum number of values live at once (including the one being defined)?

hints: A value is live from its definition to its last use.
problems.solution: After d is defined, a is dead, but b (needed by f), c and d are live: with the definition counted, the peak is 3. Registers needed: 3, though the code names 7 values.

problems.title: Launch bounds
problems.statement: __launch_bounds__(256, 3) on the GW-1 (65,536 registers per SM; per-warp allocation in units of 256, i.e. per-thread multiples of 8).

parts.prompt: Maximum registers per thread the compiler may use?

problems.solution: $65536 / 768 = 85.3$, rounded down to a multiple of 8: 80 registers per thread (80 × 32 = 2,560 per warp; 24 warps × 2,560 = 61,440 ≤ 65,536; at 88 it wouldn't fit).

problems.title: The cost of a hot spill
problems.statement: A loop body of 12 instructions runs 1,000 times. One spilled value is reloaded every iteration (an LDL hitting L1, 30 cycles latency).

options: the 30-cycle latency on a dependency, if not hidden

problems.solution: 8.3% more instructions, but if the reloaded value feeds the next instruction, the warp waits 30 cycles each iteration unless other work covers it. And L1 misses push spills to L2/DRAM.

problems.title: Rematerialisation
problems.statement: An address base + 4·tid is used at the start and end of a long kernel.

options: a register for the whole kernel

hints: Cheap values are cheaper to recompute than to keep.
problems.solution: A register held across the kernel versus one IMAD: under pressure, the allocator recomputes. Rematerialising cheap values is one of its main tools against spills.

problems.title: maxrregcount

options: Limits every kernel in the file to 64 registers per thread

problems.solution: A cap for all kernels in the translation unit; __launch_bounds__ is the per-kernel, intent-revealing version.

problems.title: Live across a loop
problems.statement: A loop keeps 4 accumulators, a pointer (2 registers, 64-bit), a counter and a bound, and each iteration loads 2 temporaries before using them.

parts.prompt: Registers live across the back edge?

problems.solution: 8 values cross the back edge; the body peaks at 10. Unrolling by 2 doubles the temporaries (and, with separate accumulators, the accumulators): the register cost of ILP.

problems.title: Colouring intervals
problems.statement: Register allocation as graph colouring: values are nodes, edges join values live at the same time.

parts.prompt: For straight-line code (interval graphs), the colours needed equal…
options: the maximum number of simultaneously live values

parts.prompt: Linear scan on straight-line code is…
options: a heuristic that can be far off

problems.solution: For interval graphs, chromatic number = maximum clique = max live, and the greedy left-to-right (linear scan) assignment achieves it. Loops and branches break the interval structure, which is why real allocators use heuristics.

problems.title: Registers versus ILP
problems.statement: A thread computes 4 independent dot-product partial sums (ILP 4) instead of 1. Each extra accumulator costs 1 register and the extra loaded operands 2. The base kernel uses 32 registers with 256-thread blocks.

parts.prompt: Is the trade good for a latency-bound loop?
options: Usually yes: 4× the independent work per warp for a modest occupancy loss

problems.solution: (a) 41 registers. (b) 62.5% (down from 100%). (c) Each warp now has 4× the independent work, which more than offsets the lost warps: Volkov again, now from the allocator's side.

problems.title: SSA
problems.solution: One definition per name eliminates false (name) dependences, freeing the scheduler; the allocator later decides which names share registers.
